items.title: Directions in a Dance
items.text:
A honeybee that discovers a plentiful patch of flowers
faces a problem. She cannot draw a map, and she has no
way to point. Yet soon after she returns to the hive,
other bees are flying directly toward the flowers. She
has given them directions by dancing.

The Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch spent years
decoding these dances, work that earned him a Nobel
Prize in 1973. He found that when food is very close to
the hive, a bee performs a round dance. She runs in
small circles, suddenly reversing direction. This dance
tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not which
way to fly.

For flowers farther away, a bee performs the waggle
dance on the upright comb inside the dark hive. She runs
straight ahead a short way, waggling as she goes, then
circles back to where she began. She repeats the
straight run and circles back on the opposite side, so
her path traces a figure eight.

The straight run carries the directions. Because the
comb stands upright, the dancer lets straight up stand
for the direction of the sun. If the flowers lie toward
the sun, her straight run points straight up. If they
lie directly away from the sun, it points straight down.
Flowers to the left or right of the sun are shown by a
run tilted the same amount to the left or right.

The waggling itself reports the distance. The farther
away the flowers are, the longer each waggle run lasts.
A run of about two and a half seconds sends the bees to
flowers more than a mile and a half away.

In the darkness, other bees crowd close to the dancer
and follow her movements before they fly out. Later in
the day, a bee dancing for the same flowers changes the
angle of her run, because the sun has moved across the
sky. The flowers stay where they are, but the dance
turns to keep up with the sun.
items.source: Facts verified against North Carolina State University Extension, "The Honey Bee Dance Language" (content.ces.ncsu.edu/honey-bee-dance-language), for Karl von Frisch decoding the dances and his 1973 Nobel Prize, the round dance for food very close to the hive (narrow circles, suddenly reversing, distance but no direction), the waggle dance for food farther away, its figure-eight path, straight up the comb for food toward the sun and straight down for food away from it, the length of the waggle run for distance (a run of about 2.5 seconds for food about 2,625 meters away), and the dance changing as the sun moves; and Wikipedia, "Waggle dance" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance), for the upright combs in the dark hive, angles left or right of the sun, followers keeping close contact with the dancer, and von Frisch as Austrian. items.title: Snowflake Bentley
items.text:
Wilson Bentley was born in 1865 on a farm in Jericho,
Vermont. His mother, who had once been a teacher,
educated him at home, and when he was fifteen she gave
him an old microscope. It was snowing that day, and his
first look at a snowflake through the lens began a
fascination that never left him.

Under the microscope, an ordinary snowflake turned out
to be a tiny crystal full of intricate detail. Wilson
tried to draw what he observed, and by his seventeenth
birthday he had made several hundred sketches. But snow
crystals do not last long, even in freezing air. At
seventeen, he asked his parents for a camera.

His father considered fussing with snowflakes a waste of
time. Nevertheless, the camera was purchased, and Wilson
attached it to his microscope. For about two years his
photographs failed. Then, on January 15, 1885, a few
weeks before his twentieth birthday, he succeeded in
making the first photograph of a single snow crystal.

His method required patience. He caught falling snow on
a tray painted black, and, working quickly, he lifted a
single crystal with a thin straw from a broom and nudged
it into position with a feather. He was careful never to
breathe on it, because his warm breath could melt it.

For the rest of his life he continued this work. He
photographed more than 5,000 snow crystals and never
found two that were identical. He also photographed
frost and dew and measured the sizes of raindrops. In
1925 he described snowflakes under the microscope as
"miracles of beauty."

In November 1931, a book of his work called Snow
Crystals was published, containing more than two
thousand of his photographs. Soon afterward, Bentley
walked six miles home through a snowstorm and became ill
with pneumonia. He died on December 23, 1931, at the age
of sixty-six. His book is still in print, and people
still call him "Snowflake" Bentley.
items.source: Facts verified against the Jericho Historical Society, "Wilson A. Bentley (1865 - 1931)" (snowflakebentley.com/biography), for his birth on February 9, 1865, in Jericho, Vermont, the first photograph of a single snow crystal on January 15, 1885, more than 5,000 crystals with no two the same, his work on rain, dew and frost, his 1925 words "miracles of beauty", the book Snow Crystals (November 1931, still in print) and his death on December 23, 1931; The Old Farmer's Almanac, "The First Snowflake Photographer, Wilson Bentley" (almanac.com/first-snowflake-photographer-wilson-bentley), for his mother, a former teacher who taught him at home, the microscope at fifteen and the snow falling the day he first looked through it, the fascination that lasted the rest of his life, asking his parents for a camera at seventeen, his father thinking fussing with snowflakes a waste, two years of trying, the tray painted black, the broom straw, the feather and not breathing on a crystal; The Public Domain Review, "The Snowflake Man of Vermont" (publicdomainreview.org/essay/the-snowflake-man-of-vermont), for several hundred sketches by his seventeenth birthday, the camera his father bought, about 2,500 photographs in Snow Crystals, and the six-mile walk home through a snowstorm before the pneumonia he died of at sixty-six; and Wikipedia, "Wilson Bentley" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Bentley), for crystals that vanish even below freezing and his record of raindrop sizes. items.title: A Part with No Lines
items.text:
When the cast list for the fourth-grade play appeared on
the classroom door, Otis read it twice to be certain.
Priya would play the queen, and Nico would play the
woodcutter. Otis would play Tree, not Ancient Tree or
Wise Old Tree, but simply Tree. His part had no lines at
all, which meant he would stand at the edge of the stage
with his arms raised from the first scene to the last,
saying absolutely nothing.

During rehearsals, the others practiced their speeches
while Otis stood with his arms in the air. With nothing
else to do, he listened to everyone. He heard Priya
rehearse the queen's long speech until it was perfect,
and he heard Nico forget the same line every afternoon:
"The crown is at the bottom of the well." Each time, Ms.
Pruitt prompted him from the front row. By the third
week, Otis could have recited every line in the entire
play, although nobody had asked him to.

On the night of the performance, the gym was crowded
with relatives and neighbors, and Ms. Pruitt was at the
back, operating the lights. In the third scene, Nico
stepped to the center of the stage, opened his mouth,
and nothing came out. The silence stretched like a
rubber band about to snap. Somebody in the audience
coughed, and Nico stared at the floor as though the
words might be printed there.

Trees do not move, so Otis remained perfectly still. A
tree, he decided, might whisper, however, so he breathed
the missing line without moving his lips. Nico's eyes
flicked toward him. A moment later, Nico announced that
the crown was at the bottom of the well, and the
performance continued as if nothing unusual had
happened.

Afterward, families surrounded the queen and the
woodcutter. At the cast party, Ms. Pruitt announced that
the tree had played the most important part in the
entire performance. Otis was fairly sure she was joking,
but he was not completely sure.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE; no real person, place or event is named.

items.title: A Listener with Four Paws
items.text:
Every Saturday at ten o'clock, a large gray dog named
Oatmeal settles onto a blanket in the children's room of
the public library. One at a time, children sit beside
him and read aloud from a book they have chosen. Oatmeal
listens patiently, and now and then he rests his chin on
a reader's sneaker.

Oatmeal is a registered therapy dog, and his owner, Pam,
sits nearby during every visit. Each reader receives
fifteen minutes. Some children bring picture books,
while others arrive with chapter books and a bookmark
already halfway through.

Why would anyone read to a dog? Reading aloud can be
difficult for children who are still learning, and many
of them feel nervous when an adult or a classmate is
listening. A dog does not interrupt. It never corrects a
mistake or laughs when a word comes out wrong. Paloma,
who is eight, puts it more simply: "He never says,
'Sound it out.'"

The idea is not new. In 1999, the public library in Salt
Lake City, Utah, held a program called "Dog Day
Afternoons," in which children read to therapy dogs, and
more than one hundred children attended. Since then,
libraries across the country have started similar
programs.

Pam has a technique of her own. When a reader reaches a
difficult word, Pam sometimes says, "I don't think
Oatmeal knows that one. Could you explain it to him?" At
that moment, the child, and not the adult, becomes the
teacher.

At a quarter past ten, Paloma closed her book, and
Oatmeal thumped his tail twice against the floor. Before
she left the library, Paloma signed up for the following
Saturday.
items.source: Facts verified against Points of Light, "Sandi Martin" (pointsoflight.org/awards/sandi-martin), for the reading-to-therapy-dogs program begun in 1999, piloted as "Dog Day Afternoons" at the Salt Lake City Library with more than 100 children, and similar programs in public libraries across the country; and the Healthy Communities Institute Promise Practice page, "Reading Education Assistance Dogs (R.E.A.D.)" (healthyneo.org/promisepractice/index/view?pid=3506), for children reading to registered therapy animals in libraries and schools and the dogs as non-judgmental listeners who ease children's fear of reading aloud. The library, Oatmeal, Pam and Paloma are invented. Original content authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: Counting to Thunder
items.text:
A flash brightens the sky, and you begin counting: one,
two, three, four. Somewhere past fifteen, the thunder
finally arrives as a long, low rumble. Without realizing
it, you have just measured how far away the lightning
was.

Thunder is the sound that lightning produces. A bolt of
lightning heats the air along its path almost instantly,
to temperatures as high as 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit,
which is about five times hotter than the surface of the
sun. The heated air expands suddenly, then cools and
squeezes back together. That rapid push and pull sends
out the sound wave we hear as thunder.

The flash and the sound begin together, but they do not
travel at the same speed. Light reaches your eyes almost
immediately, while sound moves much more slowly: thunder
takes about five seconds to travel one mile. To estimate
how far away the lightning struck, count the seconds
between the flash and the thunder, and then divide by
five. Fifteen seconds means the lightning was about
three miles away.

The sound itself contains clues. A sharp crack or click
usually means that the lightning passed close by, while
a rumble means that it was at least several miles away.

One more number is worth remembering. Thunder can
usually be heard only about ten miles from the place
where the lightning struck. Therefore, if you can hear
thunder at all, you are probably close enough to be
struck by the next flash. The count tells you where the
last bolt landed; it cannot promise anything about the
next one.
items.source: Facts verified against the National Weather Service, "Understanding Lightning: Thunder" (weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-thunder), for air in the lightning channel reaching as high as 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, five times hotter than the surface of the sun, the rapid expansion and contraction that makes the sound, seeing lightning immediately while thunder takes about 5 seconds to travel a mile, counting the seconds and dividing by 5, a sharp crack or click for lightning nearby and a rumble for lightning several miles away, thunder heard only about 10 miles from the strike, and being within striking distance whenever thunder can be heard. Original content authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: The Day Noon Came Twice
items.text:
Before 1883, Americans could not agree on what time it
was. Each town set its clocks by the sun, calling it
noon at the moment the sun reached its highest point in
the sky. Because the sun does not reach that point
everywhere at once, one town's noon came a few minutes
earlier or later than the next town's.

The differences were real. When it was noon by the sun
in Chicago, it was 11:50 in St. Louis, Missouri, and
only 11:27 in Omaha, Nebraska. In Indianapolis, Indiana,
it was already 12:07. For people who stayed in one town,
the differences hardly mattered, because everyone nearby
followed the same clock.

Railroads changed that. A train traveling east or west
passed through town after town, each keeping its own
time. The railroad companies kept separate times as
well, and by the early 1880s there were dozens of them.
Timetables were confusing, and a traveler's watch might
disagree with the clock at almost every station.

Eventually the railroads made a plan of their own. At
noon on November 18, 1883, they began using four time
zones across the country: Eastern, Central, Mountain,
and Pacific. Every clock inside a zone would show the
same time, and each zone was one hour apart from the
next.

In several cities, the clocks struck noon twice that
day, once by the old local time and once by the new
standard time, so people called it the Day of Two Noons.
Most cities adopted the new time immediately, and many
more switched within a year.

The railroads, not the government, had made the change.
Congress did not make standard time the law until 1918,
and by then much of the country had been living on
railroad time for thirty-five years.
items.source: Facts verified against the Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis, "Whose Time Is It Anyway? A Brief History of Standardized Time Zones in the United States" (blogs.loc.gov/law/2024/11/whose-time-is-it-anyway-a-brief-history-of-standardized-time-zones-in-the-united-states/), for towns setting clocks by the sun, an estimated 80 railroad times by the early 1880s, the traveler's watch at odds with station clocks, the zones one hour apart, the Day of Two Noons on November 18, 1883, most cities adopting the new time at once and many more within a year, and the Standard Time Act of 1918; Iowa PBS, "What Time Is It? Railroads Bring Standard Time" (iowapbs.org/iowapathways/mypath/2584), for clocks set at noon when the sun was highest and the times in St. Louis (11:50), Omaha (11:27) and Indianapolis (12:07) at noon in Chicago; Union Pacific, "Surprising Railroad Inventions: U.S. Time Zones" (up.com/customers/track-record/tr031020-time-zones.htm), for the four zones, Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific; NCpedia, "Time Zones" (ncpedia.org/time-zones), for the change at noon on November 18, 1883, and the importance of schedules for trains running east and west; and the University of Massachusetts Boston, "Building the World" (blogs.umb.edu/buildingtheworld/?p=13989), for local noon being acceptable within a city but not for the trains that connected cities. items.title: Notes Hammered from a Barrel
items.text:
A steel pan looks like the bottom of an old barrel with
a few dents in it. In a way, that is exactly what it is.
Yet when a player strikes it with rubber-tipped sticks,
it rings with clear musical notes.

The steel pan developed in Trinidad and Tobago during
the 1930s and 1940s, and its story begins with a ban. In
the 1880s, drumming was banned at Carnival. Musicians
beat bamboo sticks together instead, in what came to be
called tamboo bamboo bands. Those bands were banned in
turn. By the mid-1930s, players were also striking
metal: frying pans, trash can lids, cookie tins, and
paint cans.

Players discovered that a dented tin could ring with its
own particular note. A raised part of the metal also
sounded different from a flat part. Young musicians
began experimenting with discarded oil drums, and they
learned to pound many notes into the bottom of a single
drum.

Making a pan is loud, careful work. First, the maker
pounds the bottom of the drum with a heavy hammer until
it sinks into a deep bowl. Next, the notes are marked
out and shaped in the bowl. The side of the drum, called
the skirt, is cut to a length that depends on the kind
of pan. The metal is then heated over a fire. Last comes
the tuning, as the maker carefully taps each note with a
hammer until it sounds exactly right. The maker does not
add music to the drum; the music is hammered out of the
metal itself.

The size of each note decides its sound: the larger the
oval of metal, the lower the note. A bass pan may use a
whole drum for only three low notes, so one bass player
may play six drums.

Today the steel pan is the national instrument of
Trinidad and Tobago. In 2023, the United Nations named
August 11 World Steelpan Day. That is quite a career for
a barrel that somebody once threw away.
items.source: Facts verified against Wikipedia, "Steelpan" (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steelpan), for its development in Trinidad and Tobago in the 1930s and 1940s, drumming banned in the 1880s and replaced by bamboo sticks beaten together, which were banned in turn (tamboo bamboo), metal percussion by the mid-1930s including frying pans and dustbin lids, rubber-tipped sticks, "the larger the oval, the lower the tone", a bass pan using the entire drum for three notes so that one person may play six, its status as the national instrument, and the United Nations General Assembly declaring 11 August World Steelpan Day in 2023; the Horniman Museum, "The Horniman's tenor steel pan" (horniman.ac.uk/story/the-hornimans-tenor-steel-pan), for drumming banned at carnival, raised parts of the drum sounding different from flat parts, and the national instrument; Discover Trinidad & Tobago, "Origins of the steelpan (or steel drum)" (discovertnt.com/articles/Trinidad/Steelbands/136/3/19), for biscuit and paint tins that gave single notes when hammered, young players turning to discarded oil drums, and the steps of sinking, cutting the skirt, firing, marking the notes and tuning by hammering; and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers, "Engineering Musical Drums" (asme.org/topics-resources/me-today/engineering-musical-drums), for hammering the drum into a dish, forming the notes, cutting the side to a length set by the kind of pan, heating, and hand tuning. items.title: Why the Mockingbird Sings Every Song
items.text:
Long ago, only one bird could sing. Every morning the
mockingbird sang from the top of the tallest pine, and
her melody was so long that it lasted until noon. It had
a section for rain, a section for wind, and many more.
The other birds could only chirp, and they listened
admiringly from the branches below.

One morning the owl flew up beside her. "Your song is
too long for one bird," said the owl. "Could you spare a
small piece of it for me? The nights are terribly
quiet." The mockingbird was proud of her melody, but she
was also generous. She gave the owl a slow, low section
that sounded like wind in an empty barn, and the owl
carried it into the night.

The next day the oriole arrived, hoping for something
bright for the treetops, and the day after that the
nuthatch appeared, wanting only something short and
quick. All spring the birds kept coming, and the
mockingbird never sent anyone away.

Then one morning she opened her beak to sing, and
nothing came out, because she had given away the final
piece without noticing. Her heart sank. She did not
blame the other birds, since every piece had been hers
to give. Still, the top of the pine felt dreadfully
quiet, and she sat there all day with her head tucked
low.

That evening the owl began calling in the woods, the
oriole answered from the treetops, and the nuthatch
chattered from a branch. The mockingbird listened, and
slowly she lifted her head. She recognized every one of
those melodies, because she had created them. So she
sang the owl's song back, then the oriole's, then the
nuthatch's, repeating each one to be sure she had it
right.

That is why, to this day, the mockingbird imitates the
songs of many other birds, repeating each one several
times. It is also why she occasionally sings on moonlit
nights: she is still keeping track of every song she
gave away.
items.source: An original folktale. The real behavior it explains is verified against the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency, "Northern Mockingbird" (tn.gov/twra/wildlife/birds/grassland-and-shrub-birds/northern-mockingbird.html), for its imitation of dozens of other birds' songs, phrases repeated three or more times, and singing on moonlit nights; and Northern Woodlands, "The Northern Mockingbird: Master of Mimicry" (northernwoodlands.org/outside_story/article/mockingbird-mimicry), for each phrase sung several times over. Original content authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: The Frog in the Leaves
items.text:
Alaska is home to three kinds of frogs and toads, and
two of them spend the winter hiding from the ice. The
western toad spends the winter in a burrow below the
frost line, where the soil does not freeze. The Columbia
spotted frog buries itself in the mud at the bottom of a
pond that is too deep to freeze solid. The wood frog
does something stranger. In the fall, it settles into a
shallow hollow on the forest floor, beneath a blanket of
fallen leaves, and waits for the cold to find it.

The cold always does. The wood frog is North America's
only amphibian north of the Arctic Circle, where winter
temperatures of fifty degrees below zero are not
unusual. A layer of snow on top of the leaves adds extra
protection. Still, as the first ice forms in the frog's
toes and eyes, its liver begins to produce large amounts
of glucose, a kind of sugar. The sugar travels through
the frog's blood into every cell in its body.

Within a few hours, ice fills the frog's belly and wraps
around its organs. Flat crystals of ice spread between
its skin and its muscles, and its eyes turn white.
Nearly seventy percent of the water in its body becomes
ice. Its heart stops beating, and it stops breathing.
Inside each cell, though, the thick, syrupy sugar keeps
the water from freezing, and the cell survives. The frog
can remain frozen solid this way for as long as eight
months.

In the spring, the frog thaws from the inside out. First
its heart starts beating again. Then its brain wakes up,
and finally its legs begin to move. Within hours, the
males are hopping toward shallow ponds and calling to
the females with a sound like ducks quacking.
items.source: Facts verified against the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Wildlife Notebook Series, "Frogs and Toads" (adfg.alaska.gov/static/education/wns/frogs_and_toads.pdf), for Alaska's one toad and two frogs, the western toad wintering in burrows below the frost line, the Columbia spotted frog hibernating in mud beneath water too deep to freeze to the bottom, the wood frog as widespread in northern North America and the only amphibian there north of the Arctic Circle, its shallow hollows under dead vegetation with snow cover as added insulation, glucose made in the liver protecting the cells, ice filling the abdominal cavity and encasing the organs within a few hours, flat ice crystals between skin and muscle, the eyes turning white, nearly 70 percent of body water turning to ice, the heart and breathing stopping, and the males calling with a sound like duck quacking within hours of thawing; the National Park Service, Gates of the Arctic National Park, "Biological Miracle" (nps.gov/gaar/learn/nature/wood-frog-page-2.htm), for winter temperatures of minus 50 degrees Fahrenheit, hibernation in the leafy litter on the forest floor, glucose flushing into every cell, freezing solid for up to eight months, and thawing from the inside outward, heart first, then brain, then legs; the National Park Service, Denali National Park, "Amphibians" (nps.gov/dena/learn/nature/amphibians.htm), for the eyes and extremities freezing first and glucose circulating through the bloodstream into the cells; the British Columbia Ministry of Environment, "Wood Frog" (env.gov.bc.ca/wld/documents/woodfrog.pdf), for its being the only North American amphibian that occurs north of the Arctic Circle; and the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, University of Georgia, "Wood Frog" (srelherp.uga.edu/frogs-and-toads/wood-frog), for its being the only amphibian in the Western Hemisphere known to range above the Arctic Circle. The Arctic claim is limited to North America because the Arctic Biodiversity Assessment, chapter 5, "Amphibians and Reptiles" (arcticbiodiversity.is/the-report/chapters/amphibians-and-reptiles), lists four Eastern Hemisphere amphibians that also range into the Arctic, with the wood frog the only one in the Western Hemisphere. items.title: The Fastest Woman in the World
items.text:
When Wilma Rudolph was a little girl in Tennessee in the
1940s, few people would have guessed that she would one
day race in the Olympics. She was the twentieth of
twenty-two children, and she was sick much of the time.
She survived pneumonia, scarlet fever, and polio, a
disease that can leave a person's arms or legs weak or
unable to move. She lost the use of her left leg and was
given a metal brace to wear.

Her family refused to give up on that leg. Again and
again, they took off the brace and rubbed the weak leg
to help it heal. Slowly it grew stronger. By the time
she reached high school, Wilma had left the brace far
behind and had become a star on her school's basketball
team.

In 1955, a college track coach named Ed Temple came to
Clarksville to referee a basketball game. He saw the
skinny fourteen-year-old play and invited her to his
summer camp. The next year, at sixteen, she was the
youngest member of the United States track team at the
Olympics in Australia. She came home with a bronze medal
from a relay race.

Four years later, at the 1960 Olympics in Rome, Italy,
she won gold medals in the 100-meter dash, the 200-meter
dash, and a relay race. No American woman had ever won
three gold medals in track and field at a single
Olympics. Soon she was being called the fastest woman in
the world.

Her hometown of Clarksville planned to welcome her back,
but it planned two separate celebrations, one for its
white residents and one for its Black residents. Rudolph
refused to take part. Because she insisted, the town
held one parade for everyone. It was the first event in
Clarksville's history that was open to Black and white
residents together.
items.source: Facts verified against the National Women's History Museum, "Wilma Rudolph" (womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/wilma-rudolph), for her family of 22 children, polio and scarlet fever, the leg brace her family removed to massage her leg, high school basketball, the 1956 bronze medal in the relay, the three 1960 gold medals, her being the first American woman to win three gold medals in track and field at the same Olympic Games, and her refusal to attend a homecoming parade that was not integrated; the Tennessee Encyclopedia, "Wilma Rudolph" (tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entries/wilma-rudolph/), for her being the twentieth of twenty-two children and for coach Edward S. Temple seeing the fourteen-year-old while refereeing a Clarksville basketball game in early 1955 and inviting her to his summer camp; Visit Clarksville, "Wilma Rudolph" (visitclarksvilletn.com/clarksville-connections/athletics/wilma-rudolph/), for her paralyzed left leg, her place at sixteen as the youngest member of the 1956 U.S. track and field team in Melbourne, Australia, and her golds in the 100 meters, the 200 meters and the relay; Biography.com, "Wilma Rudolph" (biography.com/athletes/wilma-rudolph-childhood-health-olympics), for losing the use of her left leg and being given a metal brace, and for being called the fastest woman in the world; the White House Historical Association, "Olympian Wilma Rudolph Visits the White House" (whitehousehistory.org/olympian-wilma-rudolph-visits-the-white-house), for pneumonia, polio and scarlet fever, the town's plan for two separate celebrations for white and Black residents, her refusal, and the parade as the first racially integrated event in Clarksville's history; and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, "About Polio" (cdc.gov/polio/about/index.html), for polio causing weakness or paralysis in the arms or legs. The three-golds record is stated for track and field only, because Olympedia (olympedia.org/athletes/50967) records the swimmer Ethelda Bleibtrey of the United States winning three gold medals at the 1920 Games; several pages that drop the words "track and field" are wrong on this point. Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: The Shelf in the Hallway
items.text:
On her third day at her grandfather's house, Raina
decided to organize his bookshelf. It stretched along
the entire hallway, and it was a mess. Thin paperbacks
leaned against enormous atlases, a cookbook was wedged
between two mysteries, and a bird guide lay sideways
across a row of history books.

While Grandpa was at the hardware store, Raina carried
every book into the living room. She arranged them
alphabetically by the authors' last names, exactly the
way the school librarian did, and returned them to the
shelf one at a time. When she finished, the shelf looked
as orderly as a row of piano keys, and she sat down to
wait.

Grandpa came in whistling, set down his paper bag,
noticed the shelf, and stopped whistling. For a long
moment he said nothing at all. Then he slowly ran one
finger along the spines, the way a person might trace a
map of a town he used to live in.

"Where's the summer we drove to the lake?" he asked
quietly.

Raina did not understand, so he showed her. He located
the bird guide near the beginning of the shelf, the
cookbook near the end, and a paperback with a cracked
cover somewhere in the middle. Those three books had
always stood together, he explained, because he had read
them the same summer, the year he learned to make soup
and tell a heron from an egret. The shelf had never been
a mess. It had been arranged in the order he had lived
it.

Raina's face went hot. "I can put them back," she
offered, although she had no idea how.

"We'll do it together," Grandpa answered. "You hand me
the books, and I'll tell you where each one belongs."

It took them three evenings. When the last book was in
place, Grandpa cleared a narrow space at the far end of
the bottom shelf. Then he held out his hand for the
novel Raina had been reading all week.
items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE; no real person, place or event is named.

items.title: The Puppy Who Was Not Ours
items.text:
Our puppy arrived on a Saturday in March with a green
leash, a bag of food, and a rule book thicker than my
math textbook. Her name was Saffron, and she was not
really ours. She belonged to a school that trains guide
dogs for people who are blind. My family had volunteered
to raise her until she was old enough to begin her real
training.

Puppies like Saffron go to volunteer families when they
are seven or eight weeks old. For about a year, the
family teaches the puppy house manners and basic
obedience: sit, stay, come, and do not chew the couch.
An important part of the job, though, is something the
school calls socializing. Someday a guide dog may have
to lead its owner through a crowded store or a noisy
airport without being frightened. So the family takes
the puppy to places like that while she is young, again
and again, until nothing surprises her.

Saffron went everywhere with us. She rode in the car to
my soccer practice. She napped under the table at my
cousin's birthday dinner. At the grocery store, she
stopped and stared the first time the automatic doors
slid open. By our fifth trip, she walked through them as
if she had been doing it all her life.

The rule book never said how hard the last day would be.
When Saffron was fifteen months old, we drove her back
to the school, where an instructor would spend about
four months teaching her to guide. I held the leash
until the very end. Then I handed it over, and Saffron
trotted off beside her new trainer without looking back.
My mom squeezed my shoulder. "That," she said, "is
exactly what we raised her to do."
items.source: The narrator, the family and Saffron are fictional. Facts about raising guide dog puppies verified against The Seeing Eye, "Puppy Raising" (seeingeye.org/get-involved/puppy-raising/): puppies go to volunteer raisers at seven or eight weeks, raisers teach house manners and basic obedience and socialize them to experiences from shopping to airports, puppies return at about 14 to 16 months, and an instructor then teaches them the skills of a guide over the next four months. Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: Stone Icicles
items.text:
Deep inside a limestone cave, stone seems to drip from
the ceiling. Thin tubes and long, pointed shapes hang
overhead like icicles, and rounded mounds rise from the
floor beneath them. Nobody carved these shapes. They
were built one drop of water at a time.

The story begins above ground. As rain soaks through the
soil, it picks up a small amount of acid from rotting
leaves. This acid, called carbonic acid, is the same
thing that gives soda pop its fizz. The acidic water
seeps into small cracks in the rock below and slowly
dissolves the rock it touches. Over a very long time,
the moving water widens the cracks into passages and
rooms.

The water carries some of the dissolved rock along with
it. When a drop oozes out of a cave's ceiling, it meets
the cave's air and gives off carbon dioxide gas, the
same way an opened bottle of soda pop loses its fizz.
Without that gas, the water cannot hold on to all of its
dissolved mineral, which is called calcite. So before
the drop falls, it leaves behind a tiny ring of calcite.
The next drop adds another ring, and the next adds
another. Ring by ring, a hollow tube called a soda straw
grows down from the ceiling. A soda straw often takes a
hundred years to grow a single inch.

If the inside of a soda straw gets blocked, water begins
to run down its outside instead, coating it with calcite
and making it thicker. The straw has become a
stalactite. Meanwhile, drops that splash onto the floor
leave calcite there too, building a mound called a
stalagmite. Given enough time, a stalactite and the
stalagmite below it can meet and join into a column.

Cave visitors are asked never to touch these formations.
The oils on human skin leave stains, and they can also
waterproof the stone so that it stops growing.
items.source: Facts verified against the National Park Service, Ozark National Scenic Riverways, "How Caves Form" (nps.gov/ozar/learn/education/how-caves-form.htm), for rainwater picking up carbonic acid from rotting leaves, the same acid that gives soda pop its fizz, acidic water dissolving the rock, each drop leaving a little ring of calcite, soda straws often taking 100 years to grow one inch, a blocked straw becoming a stalactite as water runs down its outside, and stalagmites built by water dripping onto the floor; NPS, "Solution Caves" (nps.gov/articles/000/solution-caves.htm), for acidic water seeping into small cracks in limestone and dissolving the rock it touches until the crack becomes a cave; NPS, "Speleothems" (nps.gov/subjects/caves/speleothems.htm), for every stalactite beginning as a hollow soda straw and a stalagmite growing together with its stalactite into a column; NPS, Great Basin National Park, "Speleothems (Cave Formations)" (nps.gov/grba/learn/nature/speleothems-cave-formations.htm), for water entering a cave giving off carbon dioxide the way an opened soda pop does, and calcite no longer staying in solution without it; and NPS, Carlsbad Caverns National Park, "Rules for the Cave - What and Why?" (nps.gov/cave/blogs/rules-for-the-cave-what-and-why.htm), for skin oils staining formations and waterproofing them so they stop growing. Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: Ten Days to Sacramento
items.text:
In 1860, the railroad and the telegraph reached only as
far west as St. Joseph, Missouri. Beyond that town lay a
vast land of deserts and mountains, and California was
nearly two thousand miles away. A letter sent across
that land by stagecoach took weeks. Many people believed
that no one could carry mail across it all year round.

Three businessmen were determined to prove them wrong.
On April 3, 1860, they started the Pony Express, a relay
of riders on horseback. Stations stood every ten to
fifteen miles along the trail, and at each one a fresh
horse was waiting. A rider would leap down, throw his
mochila, a saddle cover with four pockets for mail, onto
the new horse, and gallop on. On average, a rider covered
75 to 100 miles a day. The first mail from St. Joseph
reached Sacramento, California, in just ten days.

Speed was costly, though. Sending a letter by Pony
Express could cost as much as five dollars for half an
ounce. At the time, ordinary postage cost no more than
ten cents. Even with prices that high, the company never
earned enough to pay its expenses, and it sank deep into
debt.

Meanwhile, another kind of messenger was on its way.
About ten weeks after the first riders set out, Congress
approved money to help build a telegraph line across the
continent. As crews strung wire westward from the
Missouri River and eastward from California, the riders
carried telegrams across the shrinking gap between the
two ends. On October 26, 1861, the telegraph finally
joined San Francisco to New York City. On that same day,
the Pony Express officially came to an end. It had
lasted only eighteen months.
items.source: Facts verified against the United States Postal Service Historian, "The Pony Express" (about.usps.com/who/profile/history/pdf/pony-express.pdf), for St. Joseph, Missouri as the westernmost point reached by the railroad and telegraph, the nearly 2,000-mile route across deserts and mountains, the belief that year-round travel there was impossible, William H. Russell and his two partners, the start on April 3, 1860, relay stations 10 to 15 miles apart, the mochila with four pockets for mail, 75 to 100 miles a day, the first mail reaching Sacramento in ten days and cutting the stagecoach time by more than half, the charge of as much as $5 a half ounce when ordinary postage was no more than ten cents, and the company falling deeply into debt; and the National Park Service, Pony Express National Historic Trail, "History & Culture" (nps.gov/poex/learn/historyculture/index.htm), for Congress authorizing a transcontinental telegraph line about ten weeks after the service began, the line joining the Missouri River and the Pacific Coast, telegrams carried only between the advancing wire ends, San Francisco reaching New York City on October 26, 1861, the official end of the Pony Express that day, and its 18 months of operation. Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: A Sunday Made of Dots
items.text:
Walk up close to a large painting by Georges Seurat, and
the people in it seem to fall apart. Faces, clothes, and
even the grass under their feet break into thousands of
tiny dots and dashes of color. Step back a few paces,
and the dots come together again into a sunny Sunday on
the banks of the River Seine, crowded with people of
every age.

Seurat, a French artist, began the painting in 1884.
Today it is known as A Sunday on La Grande Jatte.
Painters usually mixed their colors on a palette before
brushing them onto the canvas, but Seurat tried
something different. He set small touches of pure,
unmixed color side by side and left the mixing to the
eyes of the people looking. He believed that colors
blended by the eye would make a more striking picture
than paint stirred together on a palette. His way of
painting with tiny dots came to be called pointillism.

The work was slow. Seurat made many smaller drawings and
painted studies first, working out where each figure
should go. Later he returned to the big canvas, made the
outlines of some figures stronger, and added new ones,
including a monkey on a leash. The finished painting was
shown in Paris in 1886. It is nearly seven feet tall and
about ten feet wide.

Sadly, not every color has lasted. For the sunlit grass,
Seurat used a bright paint called zinc yellow. By 1892,
people had noticed that it was turning a dull brown.
Today the painting hangs in the Art Institute of
Chicago, darker in places than the day it was finished.
Visitors still step close and then step back, watching
the dots turn into people.
items.source: Facts verified against the Art Institute of Chicago's collection record for A Sunday on La Grande Jatte - 1884 (artic.edu/artworks/27992, read through the museum's public API at api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks/27992), for Georges Seurat as a French artist, the dates 1884-86, the size of 207.5 by 308.1 cm (81 3/4 by 121 1/4 inches), people of every age on the banks of the River Seine, figures dissolving into dots and dashes of color up close, the many smaller drawn and painted sketches, his return to the canvas to strengthen some figures and add others such as the monkey on the leash, the showing in Paris in May 1886, and the painting's home at the museum; the National Gallery, London, glossary entry "Pointillist" (nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/glossary/pointillist), for tiny dots of pure color that the eye fuses at a distance; Sotheby's, "Pointillism: 7 Things You Need to Know" (sothebys.com/en/articles/pointillism-7-things-you-need-to-know), for dots of pure, unmixed color meant to be blended by the viewer's eye into a more striking image than colors mixed conventionally on a palette; and ColourLex, "Georges Seurat, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte" (colourlex.com/project/seurat-la-grande-jatte/), for the zinc yellow Seurat used for the sunlit grass, its change to a dull brown, and the change being noticed as early as 1892. Original prose authored for Sheila ISEE.

items.title: Who Owns the Wind
items.text:
Long ago, in a valley crowded with windmills, there
lived a lord named Rendal who believed that everything
in sight belonged to him. He owned the castle, the road,
and every field the road touched. One spring morning,
watching the sails of the mills turn, he announced a new
rule. The wind blew across his land, he declared, so the
wind was his property. Every miller who used it would
pay him a sack of flour each week.

The millers complained bitterly, but they paid. Tamsin,
whose family operated the mill at the far end of the
valley, paid too and said nothing. Every evening,
however, she made a chalk mark on the mill door: a
straight line for a windy day and a circle for a still
one.

That summer brought a long, hot calm. For three weeks
the air hung over the valley like a damp blanket, and
not a single sail turned. When the lord's servant came
for the flour, Tamsin handed him an empty sack and
pointed to the row of circles on the door. "Your wind
did not come to work," she explained, "so there is no
flour to share."

The lord frowned at the empty sack, but he could hardly
argue.

That autumn, a storm roared down the valley, tore the
sails from Tamsin's mill, and flattened her barn. The
next morning, she climbed the hill to the castle
carrying a long sheet of paper.

"Here is the bill for the repairs, my lord," she said
politely. "Your wind caused this damage, and since the
wind belongs to you, so does the bill."

Red in the face, the lord shouted that nobody could be
blamed for the wind, because it went wherever it
pleased.

"Then it is a strange thing to own," Tamsin replied.

Before evening, the lord's messengers galloped through
the valley announcing that the wind belonged to no one.
To this day, if a traveler there asks who owns the wind,
the children point at the turning sails and laugh.
items.source: Original folktale authored for Sheila ISEE; no real person, place or event is named.
